utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I'm sure you're surprised why we asked the witness to excuse us for a short while. May we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness be brought into court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Before we begin, let me just remind you that you are bound by the oath -- rather, the declaration you made on the first day of appearance that you will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And secondly, let me just apologise for asking that you get out of court. We just had some logistical issues to deal with which were required to be dealt with without the presence of a witness in court. Thank you so much. Mr. Milovancevic, you are still busy with the witness. Thank you very much. The witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are still continuing with the examination-in-chief. I would just like to remind you that the protection measures are still in force, so please do not mention the post you were at, and if this is necessary we can always move into private session when talking about information that could reveal your identity. Once again, I would like to draw your attention to something that applies to me as well, and that is between my question and your answer we need to pause so that the interpreters could do their job. Thank you very much. At the end of the day on Friday, we came to a topic that relates to the situation in Drnis and the -- the refusal of members of that police station to obey orders. So we will continue with this topic. Can you please tell us briefly why they did that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the public security station in Drnis refused to obey orders because that evening they received an order to break up the barricades using weapons that were located on the border between the Knin and Drnis municipalities. That was the first task. They refused to obey that order and said that they did not want to resolve the problem in that way during the night because implementation of that assignment could cause a lot of casualties, that it would have been much simpler to deal with this matter in the day-time, through negotiations and talks without bloodshed, because bloodshed would then lead to a deterioration of the situation on a broader area and that would in turn reflect on the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for you to be able to orient yourself more easily, if you look at the atlas that we all have, Drnis is on page 25, quadrant E3. It's at the very bottom to the right of page 25 of the atlas. It's just below Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And since I have pointed out to the Trial Chamber where Drnis is on the map, can you please tell us how far apart Knin and Drnis are.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drnis is about 25 kilometres from Knin. The distance between those two towns is about 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the composition of the Drnis police station staff was, as far as the ethnic composition actually is concerned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, even though I'm not all that familiar with that because I didn't actually work there, but as far as I know the ratio between Serb and Croat policemen was more or less equal, and then there were also a few Muslims in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your answer when you explained that the policemen refused to obey the order to remove the barricades by force using weapons, can you please tell us who actually issued such an order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard later, from most of the employees of the Drnis police station and from what was written in the press, the order was issued by the SUP secretary, Ante Bujas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remind us again of which SUP was Mr. Ante Bujas secretary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Bujas was secretary of the Sibenik SUP, which means that he was the immediate superior both to the Knin and Drnis public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One more question on this topic and this incident. You say that the Drnis public security station was ethnically mixed. Can you please tell us who it was who refused to obey the order. Was it the policemen belonging to one ethnic group or can you please tell us what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the employees refused to implement this order except the chief of the public security station. Both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, regardless of which group they belonged to did that. And then the reserve forces also were called in from the area who were deployed at the station as reserve policemen; they also refused the order to go to break up the barricades by using weapons. Everyone except for the chief and one or two other staff members refused to carry out that order in the public security station in Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us again what the date was or at least the time period when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident in Drnis happened on the 20th or the 22nd of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Other than the situation that you described in Knin and the situation in Drnis, do you know if there were any similar events in some other areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I heard information that there was also an attempt planned to remove the barricades from Sinj in the direction of Drnis. This was in the village of Civljani or Cetina. And there was some firing, shooting there, but I think there were no casualties, no one was killed or wounded. There was shooting and police gave up their attempt to remove that barricade. This was the police from Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the Sinj police abandoned their attack on the barricade, can you please explain who was actually manning the barricades and who issued the orders for the police to carry out such an action?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The barricades --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have an objection about foundation with respect to a number of these questions. The witness has testified about where he was and what his duties were at this time. And I'm just wondering if before eliciting testimony about what was happening in other places there could be a foundation laid about how he knew -- if, first of all, he knew and then how he knew. He says: Later I heard information, and we're about to hear questions about, well, who gave the orders and so forth without any establishment of the basis of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my idea was to dwell on this as briefly as possible. I do think, however, that the Prosecutor's objection is quite appropriate. I will ask the witness how he learned what he has just shared with us about Sinj and Cetina. I did previously fail to clarify that with the witness, and I entirely agree with the Prosecutor's objection in as far as it was an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Then you can carry on and correct that mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, Civljani and Cetina -- or, rather, Civljani you say either one of those, how far are those two from Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The settlements of Cetina and Civljani are also about 25 kilometres from Knin in the general direction of Sinj. These are the most distant places still under the jurisdiction of the Knin public security station. These two places are near Sinj and they were under the Knin public security station. They were in charge of those two towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your reference, Your Honours, this is page 25 of our map and the quadrant number is E3. It's the lower right corner of the page. You will find the villages of Civljani, Kijevo, Cetina and Vrlika right there. A bit further up on the right-hand side still is Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you say you heard about this later. Who was it that you heard this from, about the move on Civljani or the move on Cetina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received calls from citizens to the station. They explained the situation. They said there was shooting. They said an attack had been launched, and this was also how I learned about this situation. Some of the police officers in my station were natives of those areas working in the Knin police station. Later on when they came to work, they explained about an attempted attack; that's how they referred to it. There was shooting against the barricade held by civilians, and then the policemen who had been sent out from Sinj later returned. This was also something you could read in the press at the time. I also heard about this from my former colleagues in Split, which is where I used to work previously. Units had been organised that were eventually sent to Sinj and then on to Cetina and Civljani in order to crush those barricades and help normalise traffic along those roads. There were several different sources for this information. It's a well-known fact. It's no secret information at all. It was a well-known fact, generally known. As for Drnis itself, I am far more familiar with the detail of that situation, the reason being I heard everything about Drnis being a member of the police committee in the Sibenik SUP. Most of the employees of the Drnis public security station which was soon after disbanded were sent to work at the Knin public security station, which is where I was. That was my station, the station where I worked, and they told me about what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say that the Drnis station, after these events which occurred on about the 20th of August, the acts of disobedience was disbanded. Who was it that disbanded the station and who sent the police officers to the Knin public security station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the order came from to disband the Drnis public security station. I'm not sure if it was sent from Zagreb or from Sibenik. Be that as it may, the station was legally disbanded. Now, what do you mean when I say "legally disbanded"? At first there was a questionnaire asking the officers if they wanted to leave the station and saying that they would be allowed to go to a different town where they would continue to work with the police forces, and saying that all those who wished to remain would be allowed to remain. Based on all of this, most of the employees declared that they wanted to go to Knin. Some ended up going to Gracac and some to Sibenik, and so on and so forth. The official decisions on their transfer from Drnis to other places in Croatia were I think signed by Ante Bujas, who was the chief of the Sibenik SUP, and this police station was under their jurisdiction as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding these events between the 17th of August, 1990, the events sometimes referred to as the log revolution, do you know if Mr. Martic had anything to do with these events? How did he become famous in connection with this date? Do you know anything about that? How did he become the public figure? I'm having some trouble phrasing my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days after the weapons were taken from the police station, there was the regular news programme on Croatian TV and a report was read out that Mr. Martic, along with three other policemen of the Knin public security station, Nikola Mamovic [phoen], Zelenbaba Milenko, and Celic Mirko, were suspended. This was hushed up at the time, and no specific reason for this was stated, but something along the lines of indiscipline was implied. The idea behind this probably referred to events surrounding the petition signed in July 1990. Immediately after this was aired on the TV news, the people of Knin and its surroundings started assembling. Rallies were organised to protest against this decision that was announced on TV that evening. I was in town myself, and I realised that people were gathering outside the police station. I went there to see for myself what was going on. At this time, a lot of people had already assembled outside the police station, quite a crowd. So I went straight in. People were swearing and protesting. They wanted to get into the police station, and they wanted to demolish this station. They were furious about the decisions. I wanted to calm the crowd. There was a megaphone inside the station, which I grabbed in order to address the people outside the station. I told them to stay calm. There was no reason for them to mount this rally. I said everything would be resolved by legal means, as any acts of suspension within any police force usually are, that this would be resolved by the relevant court. As I was trying to address the crowd, people started chanting and voicing their discontent. There were catcalls for me, describing me as an Ustasha. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Somebody switched their mike on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had only just started working there, so the treatment I received from the locals was anything but favourable, and they clearly were hell-bent on expressing that sentiment. Dr. Dusan Zelenbaba and Jovan Opacic, deputies in the Croatian Assembly from Knin, also addressed the people assembled outside the station. There must have been between 3.000 and 4.000 people there. They addressed the crowd with their political speeches, telling them to stay calm, that the Serbs would not be attacked, and that they would defend them, something along these lines. But the crowd yelled for Milan Martic to address them, to tell them himself what he felt about the suspension of himself and his colleagues. Something else that I should say is that the situation was difficult in a more general sense because there were several people inside the police station who failed to sign the July petition, the petition that was put forth in July 1990. The crowd started calling for their heads. They wanted to lynch those Serb police officers because they had not signed the petition. There was a real danger that the crowd would try to break into the station in order to get to those people and kill them. There was such a turmoil, in fact, that one of the police officers got sick. Someone stepped in to help him, but those officers that I spoke about escaped through the back door. There were journalists there, Croatian journalists, and foreign journalists, foreign correspondents as well. There was a lot going on, and I know that Martic eventually addressed the crowd. Soon after he did this, minutes after, perhaps, I'm not sure what it was exactly, but I heard him speak. I heard him addressing the crowd. Someone spread the news that an attack had been launched against Knin by Sinj. I'm not sure what exactly had occurred, but people soon dispersed. Everybody went home to get their weapons or simply to try to escape. So the meeting or the rally reached an end. The next day, in the afternoon, since Knin was the focus, not only of Yugoslav attention but of the world attention you might say, this was in the middle of the summer season and the armed conflict that was beginning to erupt caused a great amount of disruption to the traffic and along the Adriatic road, so news about this soon spread throughout the world. The next day there was a Croatian TV crew on the scene; more specifically, a lady a journalist called Heni Erceg and her cameraman Edo Picevic [phoen]. They asked to speak to me. They asked to take pictures inside the station, specifically the room in which our weapons were stored. They wanted to see what exactly had occurred and they wanted to speak to the eye-witnesses. I wasn't in the station myself, but near the station they probably grabbed hold of Milan Martic, who told them that as long as he was in charge of the police the chequerboard would never get inside Knin. The cameraman had disconnected his camera and he was shooting by holding the camera in his hand. This was aired on the evening news that day and this was a very important thing, because this was the first time that Mile Martic appeared on national television and in grand style, if I may say. Several days later at a meeting, the decision was taken to lift the suspension of the other three police officers, and it was resolved that they should go back to work as soon as possible. However, Milan Martic's suspension was not lifted, was not revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. Just a few clarifications. Witness, at the beginning of your answer you said: "Several days after the weapons were taken from the police station," are you referring to the weapons that were taken from Knin police station that you testified about last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't want a long explanation. I just want to be clear. Then you said a little later. "Officers that I spoke about escaped through the back door." Which officers are these that you are talking about? This is at page 15, line 15, starting from line 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that several police officers escaped from the station. I am referring to those police officers who had not signed the petition back in July 1990. Several persons are involved, the eight Serbs who failed to sign the petition, and the persons that I am referring to are three or four out of those eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Lastly, to you, Mr. Milovancevic, you realise the witness's answer was very long. I don't expect you were expecting such a long answer. Can I suggest that you try to control your witness and get him to be concise and to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your guidance. I am perfectly aware of the length of the last answer. The only reason is, if I may provide a brief explanation, the fact that this event was much publicised and much used by the OTP. I just wanted to give the witness a chance to tell us undisturbed what he knows about this. The remaining answers will no doubt be shorter and I will try to make sure they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what about police stations, public security stations, according to their regular job description, so to say, did they give permits to citizens for any weapons that these citizens possessed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Police stations had the authority to issue such permits to citizens, for citizens to obtain, carry, and keep a fire-arm. Most frequently these were pistols or revolvers. This also included the purchase of hunting rifles and carbines, two different categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For anyone in the former Yugoslavia, not just in Knin, to legally possess a weapon, what would this person have to do? Who would he have to address in order to obtain a permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For anyone to be legally in possession of a fire-arm, at the time there was the law on fire-arms and each of the republics had its own law. There had to be an application to a body of the internal affairs. There had to be a request as well as a reason stated for possession, why possession was necessary, and why this person was applying to get a permit. Usually this was for personal safety or for professional reasons. Merchants, cashiers, for example, or people who were political figures and there was some danger involved, these people would frequently apply for such permits. And these applications would then be considered. In the case of hunters, that goes without saying, they often applied to have hunting rifles and carbines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say an application would be submitted and then this application would be considered. This means it was at the police's discretion to decide who would and who would not be allowed to own a weapon. But there was some discretion involved by the relevant body of the SUP, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's -- yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My objection is that the question was leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, Your Honour. Indeed, it was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who decided on the issuing of these permits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organs of the interior. There were two stages, so to speak. First an application was submitted by a citizen. The relevant person in the relevant department would then submit this for processing. What did that mean? Police inspectors on the ground would then run a check, a background check, on the person submitting the application. They would check whether this person was, by nature, aggressive or prone to misuse the weapon. They would check for any previous form, previous convictions, in which case the person would automatically be ruled out from receiving a permit. There was a more general background check to vet the person for mental illnesses, mental illnesses that he suffered from or someone in his family. So this was the general background check. Once this was done, a committee would sit in Knin in order to consider all these applications and requests. At a meeting of this committee, decisions were made in relation to each of these applications. Whenever applications were granted, a list would be drawn up of the persons who received permits. This list would then be forwarded to Knin along with the entire case file and to the Sibenik SUP, and then there would be another meeting to discuss these same applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So who had the final say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of my colleagues from the Sibenik SUP. There was a special committee. So the secretary and his associates, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did the Sibenik SUP normally stick to the law when granting these applications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were lots of applications and requests being submitted at the time, but at this point in time there was an inflation even greater than would have been normal of such requests and applications. It wasn't only the Knin area, it was the Drnis area, the Sibenik area as well. Everybody would bring their weapons, and they all brought certificates certifying that they had taken an exam and that they knew how to use the weapons. Applications were piling up. I'm sure one of the items on the agenda for the committee was to review these applications for fire-arm permits. At the beginning it was easy when the applications were still few, but later problems mounted because the situation in Drnis, Knin, and Sibenik became more and more complex. In our meetings we discussed this with increasing frequency. Normally the last item on the agenda would be the review of these applications. I once spoke to the Knin secretary about these and he said: We'll talk about that next time. A week later I was there again. We went through the agenda and reached the same item again, and I asked him what we would do with the weapons because the citizens were submitting all these applications, and we were bound by the law to provide some kind of reply, positive or negative. We were bound by the law to provide an answer within 30 days of the application, and he said: If it's a Serb, don't grant it; if it's a Croat, go ahead and grant the application. I was in the minority at that meeting, and the situation was not very pleasant. It would have been meaningless for me to stand up to this because anything I said would not have changed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At the time, were people trying to obtain weapons by illegal means?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the question is vague. What -- I'm not sure what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we heard about the legal means of obtaining weapons. When I say "illegal," I mean anything else that wasn't legal. Were I to suggest anything else, the question would be a leading one. I'm asking about obtaining weapons illegally and what this witness, as a member of the SUP, knew about this. He should be in a position to know. That's what my question was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shouldn't you perhaps be asking how the people on the ground went about to obtain these weapons, rather than suggesting to him that there could have been illegal ways of doing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is there is only one way to get weapons, that being the legal way. Everything outside that qualifies as illegal. It's a broad concept. I do know that, and that's why I was trying to cast the net as wide as possible. But if you think that's a more proper way to ask the question, I can rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think so, in the light of the objection that it is vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the legal ways of obtaining weapons, do you know about any other ways of obtaining weapons? At the time, of course. I'm referring to August 1990, August and September.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout August and September 1990, weapons were the main thing everybody was talking about, and everybody was bending over backwards in order to get weapons. Nobody was thinking about buying a car at the time. That was ancient history. Weapons were the in thing to get. I remember several break-ins by unidentified perpetrators. They would break into trains leaving Split on their return to other towns in Yugoslavia. At the railway station in Kosovo near Knin and in Knin itself, these trains were broken into. The army were sending dysfunctional or old weapons to a special office in Hadzici where these were mended. Hadzici is near Sarajevo. They were sending these weapons there for this department to mend the weapons. There were two such cases where the train was broken into and the weapons were taken away. In the first case there were about ten rifles involved, and in the next case five or six, I think. This theft was reported, so I and a couple of people from the military security department went around the area trying to talk people into returning these weapons. There were several anonymous calls throughout this period of time to the police station providing information as to the whereabouts of these weapons. It took us no more than a couple of days to get these back. There was one case where we realised who the perpetrator was. We discovered the perpetrator. We sent him to the Split court, and he was tried there. People also illegally traded weapons from World War II, old weapons, German and Italian rifles, and other kinds of weapons left over from World War II. Another way to obtain weapons was for people to forge weapon permits. Whenever we granted these applications, we would always use a special form in the process. People got hold of these forms somehow or other, I don't know, and they would just fill them in. These were forged permits, and they would use these forged permits to get weapons. Weapons were sold in civilian shops. There was no one supervising the purchase. These permits would then be sent back to us to file them away and to inform us that a weapon was purchased under such and such a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave us a detailed answer to this question. Can you please give us your opinion, your impression, what was the reason for such a situation? You said that nobody bought cars, nobody bought other things, the only thing that people sought to buy were weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were living in fear for their lives and for their property. The situation was becoming more complex. The legal newspapers that were coming to Knin from all over, from Belgrade, Split, Zagreb, had information about facilities being blown up, apartments, business premises owned by Serbs or companies that had their headquarters in Serbia which were blown up in areas of Croatia on the coast or in Zagreb. Newspapers were burned from other regions; for example, in Zagreb newspapers were burned that came from Belgrade. So this also had an effect on the situation in Knin. Explosives were planted in kiosks owned by companies in Zagreb or Split. The situation was becoming more complex. People were beginning to be afraid and they wanted to obtain weapons, hunting weapons, a pistol, in order to at least have some degree of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for a break -- oh, I think that I still have some time. I thought that I had gone over the time for the break, so I was a little bit too quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, may I please ask a question of Mr. Witness at this stage, thank you, you'll get a little break this way. Mr. Witness, you spoke about guns having been removed from trains. Were these trains public trains or army trains, freight trains, what? Were there no guards accompanying the transportation of this -- these fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these were trains that were just regular trains. They were mostly freight trains, and many people who lived near the rail tracks worked for the railways. So they know what the Hadzici depot was. That was a place where weapons were being repaired. So if the military post in Split was sending weapons for maintenance or repair, they knew where this went. Before, nobody ever touched this because it was dangerous to do that. Weapons were not needed. But now with this situation that was beginning to be created, people would break in or get in there, knowing that that is where they could find rifles. I think that's the answer. Later in our actions we returned all of those rifles, the automatic weapons, and we handed them over to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. There's another question which I'd like to pose to you. At the time that we're speaking about, based on your own knowledge, would you say at the time that the number of weapons illegally secured in the hands of citizens, as known to the police and to you, would have outweighed those which were issued legally through the authority of the police and the regular way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were a lot of weapons circulating. As I said, there was even a quantity of weapons left over from World War II. People also began to make very simple bombs. They would take fuses from training bombs, they would take the chargers, and then they would -- whatever they could find. And you even had accidents. People got hurt. There was even a case that a person was killed in a field. They were trying to light a fire and happened to hit on a incendiary device that had been thrown away. People would also use trophy weapons, all kinds of weapons. People were not trained properly. The weapons were outdated. There were all kinds of different calibres. It was chaos, but mostly nothing could be done. We couldn't take measures to confiscate all of the weapons because that would pit us against the population. The situation was such that we could not confiscate weapons and get on the bad side of the people. Even the higher command was unable to take away all these weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So at that time would the people who you could not have disarmed in your own discretion, would they have had more arms than were -- than would have been in the hands of the police and the regular authorities then? Is that the scenario you were faced with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time the police carried military weapons, an automatic rifle, hand-grenades; they had all those things at their disposal. But we could not embark on the disarmament or disarming of those people manning the barricades because that would have led to a very difficult situation. I or any of my police officers or any of my superiors did not wish to disarm the people in that way. We believed - and I still believe the same thing now - that at the time the only thing that was possible was to act politically. The policy could have been devised to resolve the situation and to call on the people to return the weapons, to help to restore safety and peace. Because those people who had weapons concealed dating back to World War II, they never used those weapons or abused them, but they felt that the time had come to get those weapons out again from wherever they were keeping them in secret places. For 40 or more years the weapons were concealed, and now they were being brought out again so they could show them. They brought their weapons out, but I believe that this could only have been resolved politically. The military weapons that were taken from the railway trains was not something that we found out about with classic investigation methods. We didn't return the weapons in that way by going and searching from house to house, questioning people and so on. We actually managed to convince the people that they should return the weapons, that there was no need for them to have weapons, it was dangerous, it was a punishable act to take military weapons. So we did manage to solve two of such incidents. And through some channels, we got information about what had happened. And out of the two incidents that weapons were taken, only one case was actually prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to thank you very much, Mr. Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to her question Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, you said it was advisable in such a situation to act politically. In the second half of 1990, were there attempts to calm the situation by using political means? Were there any delegations that came? Were there talks? Was there any other way tried to resolve the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a situation - I don't know whether this was in late September or early October 1990 - when a high-ranking delegation came to Knin consisting of the vice-president of the federal government, Aleksandar Mitrovic, and some other government members, federal government members, that also included members of the republican government from Zagreb. And I remember that the minister of the internal affairs of the Republic of Croatia was also part of the delegation; that was Josip Boljkovac. And they had talks with the representatives of the Knin political authorities at the Knin fort. And I think that the meeting was organised with the objective of reducing the tensions. There were talks to dismantle the barricades, to resolve the situation. I did not take part in these meetings in either delegation. I heard about it. My task was to make sure that the meeting proceeded as it should, that they -- the participants arrived and leave the fort safely, and so on. But it's possible that more could have been done. There were no sincere calls to negotiations by either side to attempt to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time you said that the European athletic championships or competition was taking place - this was in September 1990 - do you -- in Split. Do you know anything about the security measures in relation to Knin and that area that were perhaps carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remembering that period, I know that there were two sports events held close to Knin, one was the Sinj Alka, traditional Alka games, and the other one was the mentioned athletic competition. The Sibenik SUP issued a directive to try to calm down the tensions and the situations at the barricades, to try to keep the situation as it was and not to make it any worse with the people manning the barricades. The Croatian authorities did not wish to mention that there were any unrests or that any incidents were taking place at the time when so many sportsmen from all over the world and athletes were there. They didn't want to aggravate the situation. They wanted us to maintain the situation and the calm in our territory. They didn't want us to make it any worse. At the end of the European swimming championships in Split, Sibenik asked me to allow the police from Zagreb that was deployed as security at the Split championships to pass through Knin because Split was -- the Split-Zagreb road passed through Knin. So they wanted a unit to be able to pass through Knin without any obstruction. So I reviewed the situation with my associates, the security situation on the territory of the Knin municipality, and I wanted to test through our network of people who cooperated with us what the situation was and would it be possible for this column of police to pass. And in a few days I received information back, it filtered back, that this would not be such a simple thing because the population distrusted the Croatian authorities and the MUP forces because they felt that this might be used as a pretext to attack the Knin situation and to dismantle the Knin police station, which is something that happened in Drnis. Some citizens, there was some information that there might be a clash. So all this information is something that I relayed to the Sibenik SUP chief Ante Bujas. So then they abandoned this idea. Later, when I was reading books and memoirs of various politicians from that time, Vrdoljak who at the time had some sort of post in the Croatian government. Later he was the president of the Olympic Committee of the Republic of Croatia, and later even in Spegelj's book, who at that time was the defence minister of the Republic of Croatia, it was said then that they wanted to use that particular point in time and that already a plan had been made to attack the Knin police station and to capture the station, bring new people in, and to impose order in town, quote/unquote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we're already past the time for our break, so I wanted to just thank the witness and tell him that we're going to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I've been asking you questions about traffic on the roads, so to speak, the situation along the roads in the Knin area and further afield as well. Do you know anything about the rail traffic at that time, in September and October 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, the rail traffic was running through Knin in different directions. At the outset, it all seemed quite normal. The trains were running on schedule and regularly, but there were less and less passengers. Tensions were growing and less people travelled. For the most part, people decided to steer clear of the area when travelling. There were some break-ins. I've spoken about those freight trains, but gradually, in September I believe, cases were beginning to emerge where people damaged rail tracks, smashed them, or sometimes placed obstacles on the tracks so that the trains couldn't pass. Normally there would be an anonymous tip-off to the police station, saying that mines had been laid along a certain rail track and warning that it couldn't be used for regular traffic. So trains would be stopped and traffic could not proceed as normal. There were increasing problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whenever you received these anonymous tip-offs, as police officers would you go there and inspect the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When tip-offs of this nature were received, we did the usual thing. Laying mines is a serious crime. A crime scene investigation team would be set up, comprising an operative and a forensic expert who would gather any traces left on the scene and take photographs. At the beginning an investigating magistrate would join the team and sometimes the prosecutor, but this gradually ceased to be the case and the Prosecutor stopped joining these CSI teams. Facts would be ascertained upon their arrival, and an investigation would be opened. A railroad team would be sent to this place to repair any damage, but this kept the trains waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever successful in tracking down any perpetrators in cases like these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember - and this was after all 16 years ago - I don't think any perpetrators were ever found for these crimes. This was difficult because these things always happened outside settled areas, outside any areas in which people moved around a lot. There were hardly any witnesses to speak of, and cases were left unresolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is a CSI team?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, crime scene investigation team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this situation involving the railways, did you ever contact the ministry, whatever ministry there was in Zagreb that was in charge of these issues? Was there any serious attempt to remedy the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following these events, we would immediately inform the railway administration office in Knin itself. We kept our Sibenik SUP informed as well as the MUP headquarters in Zagreb. We kept them informed about everything that we did and hoped that they would then inform the national railways. At this time, however, I remember a team suddenly appeared from Zagreb, a team of high-ranking railway officials, national railway officials, about six or seven of them, for the most part sector managers in the governing body of the Croatian national railways based in Zagreb. They suddenly appeared at the police station in Knin. I was called to a meeting. It was concluded that the railway traffic in the Knin area was not running smoothly, and this affected the whole of Croatia. They wanted to see for themselves what the situation was along the rail tracks in the area. They used a train comprising about three cars and a locomotive, and they headed for Zadar, for Kistanje. I gave them an escort comprising two or three police officers who joined them on that train. I'm not sure what the place is called, but it's about 20 kilometres from Knin. There was a narrowing of the rail track and there were rocks on the rail track which hindered their passage. Needless to say, the railway officials who were on the train and the police officers headed for that narrowing and were fired on from inside this narrowing. They did not want to run any further risks and they just went straight back. My own patrol filed a report based on what those directly involved in this event had reported, and the experts from Zagreb, the railway experts, said the same thing. They were not prepared to risk their lives, so they went straight back to Knin. Soon after their inspection, soon after their own experience of the situation, they concluded that no normal railway traffic through Knin was possible. And I think this was when it stopped, and it was only resumed after the war had ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained about the barricades and about the instructions received from the Sibenik SUP to do nothing by force, to not use force, and to only react to possible incidents. You described one such incident. How frequent were these incidents? Were there incidents occurring anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were sporadic incidents, reports of barricades, people crossing barricades, people not being allowed to pass. We received word from Sibenik sometimes that we should go to a barricade and check what was happening. I remember that once a theft was reported at one of these barricades where money was stolen from a person. We tried to find the perpetrators. So there were incidents occurring at such barricades throughout the area. Every several days there would be something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about this order or these instructions from the Sibenik SUP, as far as the barricades were concerned? I mean their instructions to the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they would ask that the perpetrators be found. They would request explanations, if any theft or any crime was reported, if property was stolen. But they didn't press that hard. They didn't press us, the police, to identify the perpetrators because they had a different way of doing this through their associates, informers. That was how they tried to identify any perpetrators, the intelligence services and other such agencies. So they did have information on people who were manning these barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct: Incidents were reported to you at the Knin station and your reactions were immediate. You would go to the crime scene immediately, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as a report was received, we would go there and ascertain the facts to the extent that we were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's good enough for my purposes. Witness, you said that in late July 1990, as a police station and in cooperation with other police stations, you provided security and a declaration was published. I want to know more about that. What about the position of the state organs of municipalities, what about their status? Did anything change in the way these functioned in relation to the republican authorities or did the situation remain unchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, following this declaration in Srb and as far as the way these bodies were organised is concerned, the situation remained unchanged -- or at least we didn't notice any major changes in terms of subordination, in terms of how the police was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between July 1990 and the end of 1990, who did the Knin police station receive their salaries from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The salaries as well as anything else that had to do with the way the station was organised, including equipment and all of our other commitments, were arranged by the Croatian Ministry of the Interior and the Sibenik SUP. We tried to do business as usual, in a manner of speaking. We received our petrol from them, all our equipment. We would send requests and we would get our supplies. Everything went on as usual. Our salaries were paid. There was a large increase in salaries in the Ministry of the Interior, and all of this was provided by the Zagreb-based MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described the situation concerning the railways. What was the public security situation in Knin itself? You were a member of the police station there. Was it better? Was it worse? Tell us something about that, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you have an unsettled situation in a certain area and no measures are taken to remedy that situation, one thing that is certain is that as time goes by the situation gets worse. In security terms, it was getting worse all the time. People were getting weapons. The authority of the official bodies and the police itself was gradually weakened. There were acts of indiscipline. Various kinds of pressure were mounting, incidents flaring up all over Croatia in towns within the Knin area and those along the coast as well, which affected the situation in Knin itself. The security situation was worsening and fear was encroaching upon the people living there, both Croats and Serbs, Croats in particular because they constituted the minority. They didn't know what would become of them the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for December 1990, we can say that the typical thing was major decisions were taken, decisions that affected the future course of events in the Republic of Croatia. Do you know which decisions I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that sometime around mid-December, perhaps about the 20th of December, St. Nikolas Day, the decision on the setting up of the SAO Krajina was announced. And the day after there was a constitutional something or other in Croatia, secession, something along these lines. I don't know exactly what it was, but I know this was on two successive days, these two decisions, the decision on the setting up of the SAO Krajina and hen soon after there was this other decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about your work, your post, in the public security station? Between mid-July 1990 and the end of 1990, did you have normal communication, you personally I mean, with the Sibenik SUP and the Zagreb-based Ministry of the Interior? Did you regularly travel to both places and go to both these police institutions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time I was appointed to my post to the end of 1990, I would go regularly or whenever needed to both places, to the Sibenik SUP and to the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb. I would go to meetings. I would go to briefings. I would go to submit reports. I would go to collect my assignments. I would go to discuss the overall situation and analyse the overall situation. So I did go regularly to both places, Sibenik and Zagreb, to see my superiors and to try to tackle problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in your post, until when, and did any changes occur throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in December 1990, I think it was in December, there was a major incident, the murder of a police officer and the wounding of another who were patrolling the area around Obrovac. It was a night-time incident. These people were members of the Benkovac public security station. A police officer called Goran Olamanja [phoen] was murdered and another was wounded. The third officer who was with them was unharmed. He was on the back seat and the perpetrators probably didn't even notice his presence inside the vehicle, and that was why he was unharmed. As soon as the next day, I received an assignment from Zadar. Why from Zadar? Because Obrovac and Benkovac, in terms of their organisation, were under the Zadar administration. I was tasked with finding an ethnic Serb and bringing him to the Zadar SUP because he was expect -- suspected of having attacked that patrol and of having murdered Goran Olamanja, the police officer who was killed, who was also an ethnic Serb. We found this person. We went through the motions and took this person to Zadar for further questioning and processing. There were many other incidents and the situation was worsening in general, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the beginning of the answer of the witness there is a part which might need to be redacted, when he mentions that he could not carry out his job anymore and mentions the post he was occupying at the time. So I don't want to repeat all of that. He wanted to be relieved because he could not go on with his job. Perhaps that part would need to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that he doesn't say what his post was at that time. He just says: I couldn't go on with my -- I could no longer do the same job. But if -- for safety's sake --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. The translation is such that it actually is all right in this situation. But in the witness's mother tongue it sounded different, but I think it will be all right for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting is standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Just out of an abundance of caution, if it was said in the witness's own language and not translated, it will still be broadcast in B/C/S. So it presents a difficulty in terms of finding where to redact, but I think if -- if we just take the indication of Defence counsel and sort of redact in that area, then we'll catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Maybe if we redact page 37 from line 14 that -- the sentence that begins on line 14 virtually up to line 20. That would cover it. Thank you very much. So it's ordered. Line 14 where it says: "This caused me to feel ..." up to "late December" on line 20. Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, from the time that you were deployed at the Knin public security station, so from mid-July until late December 1990, did you see Mr. Martic around at the time he was working at the public security station? What can you tell us about his position and his work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I saw him around, especially up until the time he was suspended. I used to see him every day. He came to work, he was carrying out the tasks given to him by his superior. I occasionally also gave him some assignments. The period up until his suspension, so before the end of August 1990, from the time that I arrived until that time, I can say that he was carrying out his tasks professionally. And there is nothing to be said about his work. He was working very successfully. He was one of the prominent inspectors working on criminal investigation assignments. As for the period after he was suspended and asked to report to the disciplinary court in the SUP Sibenik where there were proceedings against him and he did not wish to actually respond to that summons, from that time on I saw him very rarely because I was mostly doing office work. I would go for meetings to Zagreb, Sibenik, and other institutions. I didn't walk around town to be able to see him. I saw him infrequently, and when I did see him these would be very brief encounters. We exchanged the usual customary greetings mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One more question relating to this period and the Knin public security station. Sir, for years you worked in the police. How can you describe the activities of the public security station in terms of was this regular, in terms of the application of regulations? I hope that this question is not leading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comparing that period in Knin with the period before that when I was working on more or less similar work, I can say that the tasks and the work were very different. Before, I could not even imagine that I would find myself in a situation where people were freely interrupting the flow of traffic, they were carrying weapons, there were violations of law and order without any punishment. That was the situation, though, and we felt that at the time it was best for us who were employed at the public security station to work in that particular way because we wanted to avoid consequences that could then lead to even more serious consequences. It was easy to deal with consequences that were easily put right, but the problem were those that were not easily put right. So by that I mean killings and things like that. Neighbouring public security stations also had problems, the ones in Drnis and Benkovac, Obrovac. Professional policemen in other towns of Croatia also had problems because the situation was problematic there, too, because of all of these events. Like I said, Serbs' cars were being blown up, houses, shops, there were threatening messages, and this started to happen in Knin, too. What I'm trying to say is generally it was hard to be a member of a different ethnic group when you were amongst another predominant ethnic group. It was difficult to be a Serb in the police at coastal towns or towns in the interior of the republic. It was also difficult to be that in Knin. Perhaps it was justified or unjustified, but people were afraid for their lives, for their property. At that time already people had began to move away. There were exchanges of properties. Serbs exchanged properties with Croats who were coming to Knin. There were many exchanges of real estate being carried out. There were also polls whether they accepted the authority of the HDZ or, rather, the Republic of Croatia, because at that time the majority of the Serbian population was viewed as a factor of disruption, as an enemy of the state of Croatia that would be independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now when we're talking about the position of people of different ethnic groups, specifically in Knin, are you saying when you're talking about this difficult position that this was a result of the policy of the public security station or the policy of the municipality or was it something else in question? Can you give us an explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the serious or difficult position of Croats who lived in the Knin area, in the town and the municipality, was the result of the work of the public security station or the municipality or other institutions because - and I can say that on behalf of the public security station - we actually wanted to make the lives of those people easier. We wanted to protect them from any attacks, from anything, but the actual situation was very difficult. Like I said, everything that happened earlier in Croatia and around would also be felt in Knin, so it would appear in a different form in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain us what -- to us what is it that was happening outside of Knin that had some sort of effect in Knin? Can you clarify that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier I said that the persecution in real terms of that word began of Serbs in Croatia. Property was being destroyed, there were objections, open threats at work-places, at school. The overall policy was reflected in the media that bombarded the people with all of these -- this information. The media, regardless of whether they were from Zagreb, from Belgrade, from Split, always featured reports where their own people would be presented as victims, and it was not said that both were victims. The situation kept deteriorating day by day. People were trying to find a way out of that situation, and they were moving closer to their own population, going to areas where their own ethnic group was in a majority. People, Croats from Knin, were going to mostly, predominantly, Croatian towns, while Serbs I said before from Zagreb and other places were turning to Knin and other Serbian municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you, in view of the job that you were doing and the institution where you work, were you able to control this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the other staff from the public security station where I work was unable to change the situation much or control it. As I said, all of this was happening, prompted by the policy, by the writing in the press, and so on. We were defined as an executive organ, and we were acting in accordance with directives and orders from someone else. It wasn't up to us to implement any kind of policy. We didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would you say was specific for early 1990? What I mean is what would be characteristic for the work of the public security station in Knin for that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, I resigned my post. I did it orally. I wanted somebody to relieve me. On the 5th of January, 1991, when the Knin SUP was established, is a day that I welcomed with relief. When I say "relief," I mean that I had been relieved of a major responsibility in terms of not being morally responsible anymore. I assumed that -- I assumed where this could lead later. So in early January, on the 5th of January, 1991, the Knin SUP was established and the public security station Knin became part of that Knin SUP. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this sentence security station Knin and then the sentence after that, could we please redact that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the sentence -- which sentence? Yeah. Line 4 to 5 at page 43, I guess that's what you are referring to, Mr. Milovancevic? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I think you're referring from line 25 of page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Page 43, lines 3 to 5, may it be -- may they be redacted, please? Well, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who it was who made the decision to form the Knin SUP, if you know; if you don't, you can just say that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the decision to form the Knin SUP was adopted by the SAO Krajina government and that it was signed on behalf of the Assembly by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in early January 1991 the Knin SUP was formed, and you also said that up until that time the work of the Knin police was financed by the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. What happened then as far as financing was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the establishment of the Knin SUP, the financing and technical assistance that the MUP of Croatia provided to Knin was suspended. And from that time on, its work was financed by the Knin SUP. The Knin SUP also paid the employees' salaries. At the time we didn't have any budget. We had no funds. I remember that at the time people brought money from themselves on behalf of others, money that came from local communes, municipalities, other organisations, and all of that money was put into a joint coffer which went to finance our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So then the SUP of Croatia stopped financing the Knin SUP once the Knin SUP was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I'm saying. Once the SUP Knin was established, the MUP of Croatia stopped financing its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for the salaries, am I right when I say that the salaries were paid out of donations by citizens? Is that what you said? And can you just say for the transcript yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I meant when I said that they were bringing money. They were doing this voluntarily. They gave how much they were able to. Whoever felt that they could collect some money, they did that on their own initiative. They put these lists together, and they came to the Knin SUP and handed the money over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How high were your salaries and were they regular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to express that, and it's difficult to remember what the salaries were at the time. I believe they were on average about 6.000 or maybe 6 million dinars. I know that the number 6 was involved. And it wasn't a very good salary to say the least, and it wasn't regular either. But people had their own stocks that they kept and they hoped that the situation would eventually improve. They forged ahead. They kept on working in order to survive to keep their work, and they were waiting for a better future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 4th or the 5th of January, 1991, the Knin SUP was set up. Was there any change in jurisdiction in how the work was done, in terms of how the SUP was organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the Knin SUP was established, a whole number of changes occurred. The Knin public security station, the Benkovac public security station, the Obrovac public security station, Donji Lapac, Gracac, I believe Korenica as well, but I might be wrong, now became part of the Knin SUP. Their superior command was the Knin SUP, and no longer the SUP officers that they belonged to earlier, Zadar, Gospic, or wherever the headquarters used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After these changes did the police just go about their normal daily work or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Knin SUP was established - this is just to clarify the situation and how it evolved - this was a decision by the SAO Krajina Assembly, and Mile Martic was appointed head of the SUP. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm afraid we'll have to strike the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is mention here of the witness's new position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May line 23 to 24 at page 45 be redacted, please, that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, before you go on. The reference to 6.000 or 6 million dinars, is that relevant to the period of a year or monthly or -- I wonder if you could clarify or have I not got it quite properly understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the salaries, the amount you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think this will affect the answer. It was just an explanation. My question was not about the amount; I was just wondering whether it was more or less than before and was it enough to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Still, Witness, the amount you mentioned, was that a monthly amount or what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the amount that I specified, 6.000 or 6 million, that was in reference to our monthly salary, but there was the incipient inflation and zeros were added or axed on a permanent basis. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're facing the same situation as a while ago. He mentioned his salary which he received in his capacity as so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've seen that and I'm going to ask that we redact that line. May we then redact page 46, line -- the line starting at line -- the sentence starting at line 23 with the words "I know that my ..." up to the end of that paragraph, up to 47.3. And while we are on this point, I just find the difference between 6.000 and 6 million to be too wide for anybody not to be able to remember what it -- to which side it goes. If I was receiving 6 million dinars and suddenly it goes down to 6.000, they've really slaughtered me, and I should -- one should be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we remember this as a bad thing, because it was sometimes the case that in a single day your salary would go from 6 million to 6.000, or to 6.000 to 6 million. It would increase, but you couldn't buy the same thing that you bought for five times less some days before. There was a galloping inflation and we're looking at millions in terms of how salaries changed. Can get more accurate information from the witness, and it would be interesting to look at the exchange rate with the German mark. But that would be a mere waste of time. And I believe, Your Honour, you can take my word for this. It's of no consequence, and I hope that this is a sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take your word. I was just looking at the actual amount received, irrespective of what economic factors -- what impact economic factors had on it, you know. 6.000 and 6 million are just too far apart. But I accept what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, objectively speaking. But for the reasons I've stated, I did not wish to go on with that, and this strikes me as a logical line of reasoning. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a while ago you mentioned a noteworthy detail. You said that everybody, all the employees at the Knin station had the same sort of salary. Was this ever the case before and why was this the case now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just -- it's not the first time it's happened. I would just ask counsel to refrain from commenting on the evidence, which is what I think the first sentence of the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see what you're talking about. Do you understand what Mr. Whiting is saying? That first sentence, not what you said in the subsequent sentence which is a looping question, a looping statement, but that first sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I get the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did everyone have the same salary, Witness? Briefly, please, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all had the same salary because in order to set up a new institution one needs a whole series of legal drafts and provisions that do not depend on our institution. It was the job of the municipality to pass a law like that to determine ways of financing all sorts of things. I believe we all had the same kind of salary because those were donations and we needed monthly income. Everybody at the time believed that the situation wouldn't last several months perhaps, a year at most, but certainly not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police continue to go about their work? Did they continue to go about policing despite these changes in the way it was organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police pressed ahead with their work. The normal business that the police forces are normally involved in continued. I remember a dispatch signed by Milan Martic at the time. This dispatch was about cooperation with bodies under the Ministry of Internal Affairs outside the SAO Krajina. As far as these things are concerned, I believe he talked about continuing cooperation and communication and exchange of services between public security stations belonging to the SAO Krajina and police stations belonging to the Republic of Croatia. Some names were no longer to be used, names that had been specifically requested by Croatian dispatches previously, and the same applied to information involving barricades, weapons, and other such issues. But everything else, background checks on persons of interest and things like that, were to be continued in terms of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which legal provisions or laws were applied in the work of the SAO Krajina SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a continuing application of the Croatian laws, the law on public order, which was in force at the time, as well as the Croatian criminal code. There was a continuing application of all these, but in peril new laws were being drafted and passed, which only applied to the Krajina itself. At a later stage these new laws were passed and we then started to apply these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the SAO Krajina SUP, did it cooperate with other bodies of the state? Did it act in accordance with some Yugoslav decisions? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at a document on our screens. It's the 65 ter number 645. Before this document appears, I will just say this is an SAO Krajina document. It's a Knin SUP dispatch sent to all public security stations within the SAO Krajina signed by acting secretary, Milan Martic. This is about to appear on our screens. And this is about the return of temporarily taken weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have this document in front of you now. The upper left corner, the heading, can you tell us what the date is and whose document is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading reads: "Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina, the Knin SUP, the 17th of January, 1990." I think this should read "1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It says "1990." Can you just tell us what it says. Who is this sent to, this dispatch? Can you read who is stated right there as the recipient?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The following public security stations of the SAO Krajina, all, Benkovac, Gracac, Obrovac, Donji Lapac, Titova Korenica, Glina, Dvor Na Uni, Kostajnica, Vojnic, Petrinja, and Vrginmost." This is about the return of temporarily obtained or taken weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you referred to the date. The date is right there. It's a dispatch number and then the date, the 17th of January, 1990, and you made a comment about something. What was your comment about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the correct date should be 1991 as opposed to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you read the first two lines of the document itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
