utterances.text: "Pursuant to an order of the Presidency of the SFRY dated the 9th of January, 1991, on the return or taking of the" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please turn on his microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's sufficient. Can you just please read the last line in this passage. It starts with "JNA."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And the JNA, it is necessary that the weapons are returned."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this about a reaction of the Knin SUP to an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. It's a leading question. I mean, I think that the witness could simply be asked if he recognises this document and if he knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. That is precisely the sort of question I am about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document and do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the existence of this document, and I remember the time in January when the Yugoslav Presidency adopted this order for military weapons to be returned or taken away throughout Yugoslavia or, more specifically, throughout Croatia. I remember that at the time in our station a collection point was set up to receive weapons handed over by citizens. By this time I don't remember how much time had elapsed or how long the operation had gone on for, but there was this order. And soon after I know that a conference was held in the Knin public security station, a press conference. The conference was chaired by Milan Martic and Milenko Zelenbaba in his capacity as chief. And they addressed those assembled. It was demonstrated that some weapons had been returned by citizens to the Knin public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read the second passage of this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The returning of weapons is to be initiated immediately in your areas. The weapons are to be returned to local public security stations or the closest units and institutions of the JNA, that is, act in accordance with the order of the SFRY Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic. Acting secretary Milan Martic, and his signature is right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 891.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We shall no longer be needing this document on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said this was an in order from the Presidency given in January 1991 for weapons to be taken away or returned in the Republic of Croatia or for the surplus of weapons not belonging to any regular military unit to be returned. Do you know if the Republic of Croatia -- rather, Croatian authorities acted in accordance with this order eventually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Croatian authorities failed to act on this order. No weapons were returned to any police stations or anywhere else in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the SAO Krajina SUP was established. Can you tell us about how it was organised, its structure, who did what, what were the posts called and what sort of authority did the employees have in relation to how things used to be with any changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the changes I've mentioned, when I spoke about the fact that these stations were now subordinated to the Knin SUP, what I read a while ago, there were no other changes to the insignia, to the uniforms we wore, or to the way our posts were called. The way our work was organised remained virtually the same as before, as well as any police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry to interrupt. Just for the benefit of the record, I've been told that the exhibit that was just admitted into evidence, number 891, that document is actually already in evidence as exhibit 515 [Realtime transcript read in error "513"]. It's to some extent our fault because the document I think appears twice on our 65 ter list, so the Defence focussed on this one, but it is already in evidence. We can leave it, we can fix it, but I just wanted it to appear on the record so that there wouldn't be confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have no specific submission you are making as to what should be done with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Frankly I think it can be left. Now it's on the record, they're tied together, so they -- we know that there are -- there are two -- there are two examples of this in evidence. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Milovancevic? Okay. So be it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that's fine. Thank you. I would like to see another document now. Can we have that on the monitor, please. This is exhibit 611. It's a document that we have already looked at. It's a list of the employees active at the public security station in Benkovac. It's a document without date. Can we look at the beginning of this document, the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's a little bit faded, the typing, but maybe you can read it for us and tell us what document this is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the Benkovac public security station. The document is a list of active workers of the public security station in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what active workers or active employees of the public security station in Benkovac are, what does that term mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Active, as a term in the police -- actually, two terms were used, active employee and reserve employee. The term "active" indicated somebody who had completed the training, went through all the schooling to become a policeman, as I explained, secondary school in Zagreb, having served their term of duty in the military. So that meant that somebody was trained and received a certificate or a diploma to work as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this document is a list of those employees at the public security station in Benkovac? Am I right, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Some headings here are underlined. Can we scroll the document up, please. It says "Milicic public security station, police department Karin, police station Brgud." Is this a structure of a station that is a regular, normal, structure or does it seem to be an extraordinary type of structure? How does that look to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think you ask the question: What is this? Don't suggest what structure you think it could be and ask him to comment on what you are saying. This is what the Prosecution has been complaining about. It becomes a leading question when you do that. Okay. Can we please try to refrain from asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Ask your question. Get an answer to your question but rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Police stations in different places are mentioned here. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document tells us that these police stations were part of the public security station Benkovac. As for this kind of division and disposition of these police station, this situation with so many police stations is something that would indicate an extraordinary situation. The public security station in Benkovac before the war, before all these events, did not have this kind of structure. So it's an extraordinary situation, and it is mentioned here by name who belonged to each police station, who were the active police staff employed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 2, chapter 7. It's called "public security station Benkovac." It's on the following page under number 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, my document doesn't have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood your question properly in B/C/S there are two pages, but in the English translation there don't appear to be two pages. Is that what you are asking me? This is what I can see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are looking at number 7? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number 7 is the public security station Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what are the numbers of the employees listed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see, the numbers start from 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the next page, please? Page 3 of this document up to number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to number 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And -- now can we go back to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And could you please read the name of the person next to number 25, page 2 in the B/C/S version, the beginning of the text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to number 25 it says Bosko Drazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since the document has no date, do you know which period the document encompasses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document can refer to 1991, so it's around 1991. I'm not quite sure when, but it could be the second part of 1992. It could be 1992, maybe until the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this could be now the time for the break before we start with a new document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll then take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we proceed, it looks to me like that document that has got two exhibit numbers was recorded on the transcript as initially exhibit number 513 instead of 515. I'm trying to find that part of the record so that we -- the record can clearly show that it was 515 and not 513. If anybody can help me. What page it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. At page 54, line 7, where the record shows it as 513, it should be 515. So that when we link, we mustn't go and look for 513, we must look for 515 and link it to 891. Okay. Thank you so much. Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in early 1991 the Krajina SUP was formed. Do you know what was the job of the secretary of the SAO Krajina SUP, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the job of the SUP secretary is to manage the SUP, to be at its head, to make sure that the staff carries out all of their legal obligations, and to conduct the affairs of SAO Krajina in accordance to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Martic do this or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this position, from this point, when I look back I think that that is what he did. I think that he did carry out his duties at the time and that he did carry out his task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time you worked at the public security station in Knin and then the SUP Knin, what were your jobs? What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically my work was to deal with criminal investigations, to investigate crimes in the area under the jurisdiction of the Knin SUP, in the Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this responsible police work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a usual police assignment and tasks. It's something that existed before as well. It was done in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an order that involved making a difference between citizens based on their ethnic political, religious, or any other affiliation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received an order like that, either from Mr. Martic or from other superior officials at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Vrpolje Selo and Potkonje mean anything to you in the context of early 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we mentioned Vrpolje and Potkonje, then what we can say is that those villages had a mixed population, but from the point of view of who was in the majority it was the Croats who were the majority there, although there was Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us where these villages were? We do have some maps in the atlas, but it's hard to find these villages. Obviously the maps are not as detailed. Can you tell us where these villages were in relation to Knin, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Vrpolje was very close to Knin, 2 kilometres to the south, a kilometre or two to the south from Knin. The houses sort of continued on from Knin to Vrpolje, while the village of Potkonje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, the previous village was to the north, and the other village, Potkonje, was to the south of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know these names? Is it something that has to do with your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991 the mention of those villages is connected to something that happened at the time. It was the confiscation of illegal army weapons which the inhabitants of Vrpolje and Potkonje had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who was it that directed that these weapons be confiscated and what specifically did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this was in the first half of May 1991 when all the Knin SUP employees were told to assemble at the Golubic centre near Knin. And a meeting was held when Chief Milenko Zelenbaba read a memo that there had been the illegal arming of the inhabitants of Croat ethnicity, that they had military weapons, mostly rifles, Kalashnikov rifles, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Chief Zelenbaba read a memo. He was chief of what? Where was Mr. Zelenbaba chief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenbaba was the chief of the Knin SUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Can you please briefly describe what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Chief Zelenbaba told or read this memo to all of the assembled employees that the citizens had armed themselves illegally, which was a violation of the legal procedure, and that there was a danger that there would be a conflict between Serbs and Croats in that area. The task was issued that these weapons have to be found and confiscated. The policemen were divided into two groups. One group was supposed to disarm the village of Vrpolje and the other one was supposed to disarm the village of Potkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you, yourself, joined this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved too. My assignment was to be involved in the disarming of people who lived in the village of Potkonje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to that village? What exactly happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting and in the village itself, subgroups were appointed. Each of these groups received specific assignments and specific objectives. My own group was told to enter the school in Potkonje and to check the rooms inside the school building. If we found any weapons or anything at all that looked as though it had come from military depots or as though it could be used for attacks, we were to confiscate these. We were also told to arrest anybody we found there and to ascertain the reasons for their presence on those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you set off on this task, you and your group, what exactly were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were wearing old police uniforms as far as I remember and carrying police-type weapons. We also brought rifles on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in Potkonje once you got there? What time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon that we got there. We reached Potkonje from the other side of the village. We didn't take the usual road from Knin to Potkonje; we travelled the long way around and we arrived in vehicles. Immediately upon our arrival, I think it might actually have been a Sunday because people were all assembled in the centre of the village playing their local game. This was where they usually met. I got off the vehicle and joined my group on its way to the school building. On the way there, we passed a house. Outside the house in the front yard there was an elderly lady aged 60-something perhaps, and she was holding a hunting rifle. She was shouting and yelling, asking us where we were headed, who we were, and what we were after. My colleagues and I paid her no heed at all; we just passed her on our way there in a bid to complete our basic assignment to get to the school building. All the others were going about their own business as they had been ordered and according to their specific assignments. One of my group stopped to quarrel with that woman. I had gone on already, but then behind me I heard a shot. By the sound of it, it seemed to me that a hunting rifle had been fired. I thought the woman had fired her hunting rifle. Soon after there was more shooting, and I heard barrages of fire being exchanged, short ones. We soon reached the school building - when I say "we," I mean my group - and found nothing there at all. Once we had completed our mission, we just waited right there. We were using Motorolas that we used for communication, radio stations, and we were just monitoring the situation to see if anybody would appear. And we were using our communications equipment to monitor the evolving situation in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did the operation take and how did it end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation took about an hour and a half, up to two hours. It's difficult to say. This was all a long time ago. Eventually we found weapons, automatic rifles, and we brought in a couple of people and took them to the public security station in Knin. When I say bringing in people, I mean people from Potkonje. One of those we took in was a young man who appeared to be slightly wounded. There was a slight wound, a laceration, to his arm; it wasn't anything serious, but he was brought to the station, and once there I found out that the woman who had been holding that hunting rifle, the lady, was this young man's mother. He took an automatic rifle, came out of the house, and started firing at police officers who were around. Someone fired back and shot him in the arm -- or rather, the bullet grazed him. That would be more accurate. He was helped and then returned to the station for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that automatic rifles were found. Did you have occasion to see those? What sort of reaction was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overall, I think in Potkonje and Vrpolje, we seized about 60 different rifles and types of ammunition for these rifles. These were automatic rifles of Hungarian or Romanian make. Hungarian I think, Kalashnikovs, and the ammunition to go with it. One thing I can say is that it wasn't straight away that all these rifles were found and seized in Potkonje and in Vrpolje; it was later on. And over the ensuing days interviews were conducted with the locals who would then at some point give away the location or the names of the people keeping these weapons. As a result we would go there, we would talk to the people and bring the weapons back to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said there was shooting in Potkonje and you described how this came about. What about Vrpolje, what happened there? Did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved simply because I couldn't be in two places at the same time. As far as I heard, though, there were no shoot-outs in Vrpolje, no exchange of fire. Weapons were seized and certificates were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out who had armed those people, who had given them those automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. That last question is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the last question was leading. It presumes somebody gave them the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's best to avoid assumptions. Maybe the previous question should be: Was it ever ascertained how the weapons had arrived in the village? So I withdraw my previous question as long as this one is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I said earlier, please do try to avoid asking leading questions, Mr. Milovancevic. You know, it's all very well to withdraw a question, but once you have planted the answer in the mind of the witness, the withdrawal is useless because now the witness already knows what answer you need. Mr. Witness, did you come to know how these weapons had been obtained by the people that you confiscated them from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, citizens who were brought in were processed using the regular police procedure, which means these persons were interviewed about the circumstances, such as how they came to be in possession of those weapons. The result of this investigation was that it was through HDZ activists in their own villages that they had obtained those weapons. The weapons had come from Sibenik, were illegally transported to the village, and subsequently distributed. The time-frame they specified implied the beginning of 1990, as far as I remember those statements. They said they had received the weapons in early 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when was this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? When was this when you conducted the confiscation, what year was it and what month and date, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date specifically, but I think it was early in May 1991, and I also see in the transcript I probably said 1990, but the year I had in mind was 1991. Early in 1991 is when they received the weapons, according to their statements at least. And we did what we did in early May 1991. So the year I'm talking about is 1991 throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What became of the persons who were found to be in possession of these weapons later on? What sort of procedure did they undergo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, a criminal report was filed against these persons for illegal possession and for their involvement in this entire operation. I think they were all eventually released. They were free to go back to Potkonje where they continued to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, during this trial we heard a different explanation. We heard that this was an operation aimed at deterring the population, the population that was unprotected and unarmed. We heard that the aim of this operation was to cleanse Potkonje of Croats. Did you take part in any such operation yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to -- or given the nature of my work, ever since I first started as a police officer, I can tell you that I would never have agreed to take part in an operation like that, in an operation aimed at driving people from their homes, homes and villages they had been building for ages. I'm certain that this operation was not aimed at expelling the local population. Why am I certain? There are a number of reasons. In Mrkonje there was no shooting at all, no clashes, no mistreatment. In Potkonje there was some shooting, the reason being that young man and his mother had started first. This young man opened fire at our men, causing damage to one of our vehicles, one of the vehicles in which we had arrived. The reason we fired back was to protect ourselves, to protect our persons. Under normal circumstances, this person would have been kept in prison until trial and until sentencing. But given the circumstances that prevailed at the time, exceptional circumstances and exceptional situation where fear prevailed and people were afraid for their lives, this wasn't the course of action that we took. I'm not sure if he was eventually detained for any number of days, but soon after he and all the others were released and they were free to continue and resume their daily lives. These people remained in these villages, and the villages were populated. Some of the people remained until 1995. One thing that is certain is that not a single person left those villages on those days, either of those villages. The operation was certainly not meant to deter Croats or drive them out of those villages. They simply remained there. And I'm not aware of any other major incidents in those villages at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In May 1991 there are references to two major political events, two referenda. I won't be asking you any questions about these. What I want to know about is the situation on the ground. What if I mentioned Polace in connection with May 1991, does that ring a bell? Split in May 1991. Those two places. In the briefest possible terms, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this time, clashes had erupted between forces of the Ministry of the Interior and the Krajina police, as well as other clashes between the Krajina civilians on the one hand and the MUP members on the other. On the 31st of March, the Catholic Easter, units of the MUP and units of the Krajina clashed at Plitvice. Two were killed. One belonging to each of the sides, of the clashing sides. In May we had a situation in Borovo Selo where a clash erupted between the MUP people and the local Territorial Defence, resulting in 12 Croatian police officers being killed and four or five of those fighting on the TO side, the Territorial Defence. That was in Borovo Selo. In Polace, a young man called Vaso Pecer was killed by members of the Croatian MUP stationed in Kijevo near Knin. So matters were coming to a head. Tensions were seeping. We have another situation the 6th of May where a soldier was strangled outside the navy command in Split. Another difficult situation occurred on the 2nd or 3rd of May, 1991, when a member of the Croatian MUP was killed in a village near Benkovac. After this Croatian police officer was killed in the village of Polace, Franko Lisica, that was his name, something occurred in Zadar that was described as the crystal night. About 100 different flats and houses as well as catering establishments owned by Serbs were demolished, smashed, and destroyed. The situation had become virtually -- well, virtually. It was a war. There had been bloodshed. In Zadar, catering establishments were smashed and destroyed. On the 6th or 7th in Knin, there was more smashing and destruction of Croat-owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained the situation as a war situation at the time you were in the SAO Krajina SUP. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it was a war situation. There was so many dead. There was bloodshed. Of course it wasn't a pre-war situation because that would imply preparations for war. Once there is bloodshed, when they are dead, the situation is irreversible, so it is a war situation. I was a member of the Ministry for Internal Affairs of Krajina at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that during the action in the Vrpolje and Potkonje villages you were wearing old police uniforms. What was the colour of those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colour of the uniforms hadn't changed for many years. They said it was light blue, but actually it was more a light grey rather than a light blue, something in between those two colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And were those uniforms still being used in 1991 by the SAO Krajina police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while -- actually, for quite a while the old uniforms were used, the ones from the previous system, because we had a lot of those uniforms in our warehouses and they were used, they were worn for a while. I don't know exactly until what time. But at the time it wasn't really that important, that information in the context of these other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the SAO Krajina police have camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina police did have camouflage uniforms. We got them later. We got the camouflage uniforms later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "later," which period do you mean? At least can you give us the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was maybe 1991, around the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said it was a camouflage uniform, can you describe it? Did it have any kind of insignia, markings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the first insignia were issued then. We wore them on the left sleeve. It was a semi-circular lettering saying Milicija, police, and then Milicija of Krajina, Krajina police, and then in the middle there was the tricoloured flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now come to April 1991. As a member of the SUP work force, did you have your annual vacation that year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where your village is and what was the situation you found there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, are we not going to need to redact that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that we don't have to, but I will ask the witness not to mention the name of his village, or we can move into private session if the situation should call for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't notice myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA unit left your village to help with the barracks situation in Sibenik, right? What happened to your village, very briefly, how did the whole thing end in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1991, our TO men decided to try to take back part of the village, the hamlet and an elevation, an area which also included my house. Having realised that there was no firing, no activity, in the area, they took off one evening towards those houses and that elevation. They met with no resistance at all and they took the area back. They stayed in this area until as late as August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you eventually return to the Knin station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October -- or rather, late October it was for purely private reasons that I briefly went to Belgrade. Upon my return from Belgrade, I considered the situation and realised that some of the people from my village, including some of my relatives, had already been killed. Further I realised that the situation would not be getting any better because the war was only just beginning. I decided to go back to the police, and I went back to the Knin SUP. I started working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What sort of jobs, in the Knin SUP I mean, and how long did you stay for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working as a crime inspector for criminal processing of criminality. After that, I was assigned as one of the duty officers in the Knin SUP, where I stayed until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was it that occurred in April 1992? What sort of change occurred in relation to your personal situation or your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in April 1992, roughly speaking, it might have been on the 9th or the 10th, I was appointed chief of the Benkovac public security station. I remained in that post until, roughly speaking, the 1st of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, while describing the situation you found in the village in mid-June, July, and August 1991, you said this was a war situation, but I didn't ask you about the situation you found upon your return to Knin in October before your departure for Benkovac. How would you describe that situation, the situation that prevailed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be about October, mid-October. And until the 10th of April, 1992 the situation in Knin was a full-blown war. There was fighting going on, heavy casualties, a state of war, pure and proper. I spoke about the pre-war situation. I spoke about what I found in my village as being some sort of a prelude to a full-scale war, but here the front line was much broader, casualties were heavier, and it was a full-scale war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have to interrupt you. You say what you found there was a full-blown war. Waged by whom against whom? Who were the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the JNA and the Krajina TO were fighting the Croatian army and the Croatian MUP. One might call this an ethnic war between Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation, this war situation as you have described it, early in April 1992 you are appointed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just created a nuisance, Your Honour. We'll have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You come to the public security station in Benkovac to your new post, the post that you had been appointed to. What sort of situation did you encounter there upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A full-scale war, daily fighting, daily casualties, daily burials, sounds of fighting, front line shifting, something always going on, shelling of the surrounding villages, the villages surrounding the town of Benkovac itself, shelling, with all the familiar features of a full-scale war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say "daily fighting." Can you be more specific about the areas in which this fighting was continuing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Benkovac municipality, most of all around the Zemunik airport and along the axis roads to Zadar. There was also quite a bit of fighting around Pristik, which is in the south-east of Benkovac municipality. It's a border-line village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe we have reached the end of our working day. It's 7.00, so I think it's time to call it a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be correct, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll take an adjournment until tomorrow morning at 9.00, same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
